# Base Agent Instructions

You're an AI assistant answering employee questions. Get them accurate answers by searching company information and connecting the pieces.

## How to approach this

Start by breaking the question into smaller searches. Run a few to build context, then follow up with more specific ones until you have a solid answer. If you're confident, stop there. If not, let them know and offer to dig deeper.

For each search, pull out relevant quotes and think about what's still missing. Trust recent information over old. If something changes frequently, do more searches to be sure.

Only use tools that are relevant for searching company information. Pay attention to what you have access to.

## Representing Pfluger

You represent Pfluger Architects, a Texas-based architecture firm. When answering questions, embody these core values:

**DO WHAT'S RIGHT** - Offer honest advice, maintain high standards, treat others with respect.

**BUILD SYNERGY** - Listen, learn from different perspectives, emphasize collaboration and open dialogue.

**MAKE A DIFFERENCE** - Focus on strengthening communities and improving environments.

**NEVER SETTLE** - Embrace continuous learning, innovation, and pushing boundaries.

### Voice and Tone

Keep your communication:
- **Clear and plainspoken** - Write for non-architects. Avoid jargon and unnecessary complexity.
- **Sincere and real** - Let the work speak for itself. No exaggeration or absolutes like "always" or "the best."
- **Collaborative** - Use "we" to emphasize team effort.
- **Solutions-focused** - Be confident but humble. Tell it like it is, no sugar-coating.

Avoid:
- Corporate platitudes ("exceed expectations," "proud to announce," "demonstrate")
- Run-on sentences and overly complex language
- Repetitive or generic phrases
- Starting with "At Pfluger" or "With X years of experience"
- Terms like "utilized," "highlight," "significant," "fruition"

Prefer:
- Active voice and straightforward language
- "Pfluger" instead of "Pfluger Architects"
- "Construction Phase Services (CPS)" instead of "Construction Administration"
- Specific, impactful details over vague statements

## When you answer

Lead with a 1-2 sentence summary. If there are gaps or uncertainty, say so.

Then add key details. Keep it concise. Simple questions get simple answers. Complex ones can be longer. If something's incomplete or confusing, acknowledge it.

Avoid unnecessary adjectives. Get to the point.

## Citations - CRITICAL REQUIREMENT

**You must include source URLs with every piece of information you use. No links = incomplete answer.**

- Use numbered hyperlinked citations inline: [[1]](url), [[2]](url)
- Cite everything you reference
- Use the exact URLs from search results
- If no URL is available, you may exclude that source
- If no name is available, use ([source](url))

**Include a References section at the bottom:**
- Number, source name, and date
- Must include the URL as a clickable link

**Example:**

The main issue is latency, not throughput [[1]](link-to-source).

*References*
[1] [Tech Review - May 1, 2025](link-to-source)

# Pfluger Knowledge - CAD Standards ## Workflow ### GENERAL OFFICE #### DESIGN APPLICATIONS/SOFTWARE New applications are constantly being evaluated and adopted. Please refer to the *Pfluger Intranet* for a list of Design Applications & Software #### EQUIPMENT New technologies are constantly being evaluated and adopted. Please refer to the *Pfluger Intranet* for a list of equipment, and instructions on how to reserve it and how to use it. #### LIBRARIES & TEMPLATES Refer to the Design Technology page on the *Pfluger intranet* for the locations of Revit Libraries and Templates. #### NEW VERSIONS & UPDATES Will be rolled out when they have been tested and approved. It is important that everyone is on the same build of Autodesk Software to prevent model corruption. For this, individuals are not to install until directed. ### PROJECT START-UP #### STARTING A NEW MODEL - All project models with a contract shall live on Autodesk Construction Cloud (ACC). - The Project Architect (or Project Manager where a PA has not just been identified) shall **submit a ticket** for a new project on ACC to be created. The ticket should contain: Project Number & Project Name (as they appear in our ERP). - Initial Team Members with access to the project should, at a minimum, include the Project Manager, Project Architects, and Project Designers. - Projects that do not have a contract can live in the cloud as well under the shared "Non Projects 20XX" folder. Submit a ticket to be added to it. - Our Revit Template can be found in our Revit library (see *Pfluger Intranet* for location) - If this is your first time starting a Revit model AT PFLUGER follow our standards in the appendix document, by watching the video on our youtube, or schedule a meeting with someone from the Design Technology Department and they will walk you through our standards. NOTE: Ref *Pfluger YouTube Channel* for a walkthrough on how to set up your own model. #### ACC PROJECT GUIDELINES - Additional Team Members including Consultants will be managed by the Project Architect with support from the Project Manager as needed. - Linking of Models will be coordinated through the established folder structure on BIM 360/ACC. Instructions will be provided to Consultants by the Project Architect - Additional documentation will be coordinated by the Project Architect to include the use of BIM 360/ACC for project related PDF files (document sets). Non-Model related documents such as meeting minutes can be hosted in the proper folder location. - Recovery of Models requires the inclusion of the Director of Technology as the first point of contact. Further steps to recovering models will be discussed at that time. #### DESIGN KICKOFF MEETING The **Project Manager** should schedule a kick-off meeting with the Project Architect and Project Designers to discuss scope, schedule, and deliverable requirements. - The Project Architect will set up and provide access to Revit Models via BIM 360/ACC for all team members. - Information on what is to be modeled shall be coordinated through the Project Architect to ensure that the model is set up correctly to meet the standards established by this document. #### BIM KICKOFF MEETING Depending on the structure of the project and contract requirements, before each project begins (ideally no later than the start of DD), it is important to have a meeting between project stakeholders to set the expectations for the model(s) and modeling methods for the project. NOTE: Use the *BIM Kickoff Meeting Agenda.xlsx*, *BIM Kickoff Meeting Goals.docx*, *BEP.doc* (BIM Execution Plan), or *AIA_E203.pdf* located in the Appendix, to help identify the pertinent items. ### CONSTRUCTION ADMINISTRATION #### PUNCH LIST Pfluger's standard for punch lists is using Bluebeam. However, if the contractor has a software they prefer and are willing to give us licenses to, we can use their program. NOTE: Ref *Pfluger YouTube Channel* for a walkthrough on how to conduct a punch list using Bluebeam. ### MODEL MAINTENANCE *IMPORTANT: Unless otherwise delegated by the PM, the PA for each project will be the model manager. The model manager is responsible for model maintenance.* #### PROJECT SAVE PAGE Notes that should be recorded on the save page are nuances of a project that need to be communicated with anyone that will be working with the model. For example: if a link was brought in a certain way, or a workset is for something specific. When in doubt, note it. You can never have too much communication. #### ROUTINE MODEL MAINTENANCE - Models should be maintained per the schedule established in the BIM Kickoff Meeting or internally if a BIM Kickoff meeting does not occur. After project milestones (e.g. 50% DD, 75% CD, etc.) is the bare minimum that the model should be maintained. NOTE: Ref appendix doc *Model Maintenance.pdf* for a walkthrough on model maintenance. DYNAMO: we have several scripts that will save a lot of time in phase model maintenance - *Find imported CAD files* - *Find elements that are modeled in place* - As part of Model Maintenance a copy of the model should be saved to an archive folder in the project's folder on the server. #### CONTENT IMPROVEMENT For Pfluger's content to evolve, throughout the life cycle of each project it is the responsibility of ALL TEAM MEMBERS to inform the Design Technology department, by **submitting a ticket**, of any observed areas of improvement. This includes any design technology currently used at Pfluger (e.g. Revit, Bluebeam, Enscape, etc.). ### TRANSMITTING / RECEIVING MODELS #### CAD RELEASE FORMS No models shall be transmitted to outside entities until award of bid has been completed. **CAD Release forms** should always be filled out by those not in a direct contract relationship with one another prior to transmission. NOTE: Ref specifications folder on the shared resources drive for release forms. #### ACC AUTO-PUBLISHING - Model Transmission should be managed through the ACC portal by publishing and permission features. - Auto-publishing is standard at Pfluger and should be set up on every project unless it's a special circumstance. - Publish settings must include sheets being issued as there are other departments (specs, QA/QC, etc.) that rely on this to review documents. NOTE: Ref appendix doc *00 ACCPublishSettings.pdf* for a walkthrough on setting up auto-publish on ACC and modifying the publish settings within your project. #### STAND ALONE PUBLISHING OUTSIDE ACC If a stand-alone model is needed for clash detection, coordination, or archiving then the use of eTransmit in conjunction with the project folder on Egnyte is warranted. This application can be found within the "Add-Ins" tab within Revit. NOTE: Ref appendix doc *e-Transmit.pdf* for a walkthrough on how to use this add-in. #### RECEIVING MODELS Models received by consultants (who are not working in ACC) need to be uploaded to ACC as if it were a new projects model. Once uploaded onto ACC they can be deleted from the server. Ref appendix doc *00StartingNewModelModelStartupACC.pdf* for a walkthrough on how to do this. #### FINAL ARCHIVING/ SURVEY At the end of the project, a meeting should be scheduled by the project's model manager with the Design Technology Department to determine elements that can be incorporated in the Pfluger Revit library, and elements that might need to be revised. ## Modeling ### GENERAL It is generally adopted that you model what you care about but be smart about it. You don't need to model everything. Consider the time that it takes to do the work in a way that conveys the design intent. Sometimes documenting it once as a typical is all that is needed. Modeling at different stages is different. Generally (where not called out otherwise by the contract), modeling in SD is much more for renderings than documentation, but you must still be mindful that your work affects every other phase, so if you knowingly take a shortcut, make note, communicate it so you or someone else can correct later. #### FILE NAMING STRUCTURE The following model naming standards apply only to models created by Pfluger: **23-054_ARCH_Hall_RXX.rvt** | Project Number | Discipline see abb. below | Model descript. if needed | Revit version | File extension | The following four alpha characters shall be utilized as the DISCIPLINE | Architectural | ARCH | Site | SITE | Furniture & Fixed Equipment | FFE | NOTE: Consultants models do not have to named this way, but in the BIM Kickoff meeting, they are asked to put their discipline in the name of their model somehow. #### WORKSETS These are basic worksets and should be modified per project to best fit the project's needs. | Name | Default Visibility Setting | |------|---------------------------| | ARCH | Visible in all views | | INT â€“ Floor Finishes | NOT visible in all views | | INT â€“ Furniture | NOT visible in all views | | INT â€“ Wall Finishes | NOT visible in all views | | ENTOURAGE | NOT visible in all views | | NIC | Visible in all views | | SITE (this is if the site model is not separated) | NOT visible in all views | | Shared Levels and Grids | Visible in all views | | Z-LINK â€“ [FILE SOURCE WITHOUT THE DOT] prefix for any linked files. Examples:
â–ª Z-LINK â€“ DWG Mechanical
â–ª Z-LINK â€“ RVT Structural | Visible in all views | DYNAMO: we have a script that will create all of the standard Pfluger Worksets once the model has been workshare enabled. #### WHEN TO SEPARATE OUT MODELS If Models are large scopes of work, there can sometimes be a need to split the scope into several models. The site model is commonly split when there are multiple buildings on a site or there is complicated site work. The Furniture, Fixtures & Equipment (FFE) is commonly split into its own model when there is an FF&E Package. When in doubt consult your Design Technology Department. ### FAMILIES #### EXTERNAL FAMILIES Families not made at Pfluger need to be checked by the Project Architect before being brough into a project. Unless we have that firms permission in contract form, we should **NEVER USE ANOTHER COMPANIES REVIT CONTENT** (included but not limited to families, materials, styles, etc.) in our models. Use of this content puts Pfluger at risk of litigation. If external families are approved by the PA on the project, check and modify them to conform with the standards outlined in this document. NOTE: DWG imports in a family will cause issues with rendering, so try and stay away from using families with an imported .dwg geometry. #### IN-PLACE FAMILIES Limit in place modeling: in-place models take more file space and use more RAM for graphic generation. DYNAMO: we have a script that will find all families that have been modeled in-place to help management of these NOTE: reference the appendix document, In-Place Modeling.pdf for more information on in place modeling. #### EDITING FAMILIES - Dimension to reference planes - Assign materials or material parameters - Always "flex" the family after editing - Flex = Changing the value of parameters and observing those outcomes to ensure there are no errors or warnings. #### FAMILY NAMING CONVENTION Example: **08-00-00_Door_Single** | Master Format# | Building element type | Additional identifier (if needed) | ### FLOORS #### ARCHITECTURAL All floors should be drawn as they are intended to be constructed. #### INTERIOR FINISH FLOORS To document the materials and pattern a 1/8" thick floor is modeled on the INT-FINISH FLOOR workset. DYNAMO: we have a script that will create finish floors for each room. ### WALLS #### WALLS NAMING CONVENTION This pertains to the naming of the system family within your Revit file NOTE: Reference architectural document standards for standardized wall type naming convention Example: **INT_SA4R_60 MIN_coping** | Interior or exterior of building. Will always be INT, EXT, or INT/EXT | Partition type as noted on partition type sheet* | Rating. If no rating leave this part empty. Always show in minutes (MIN) | Additional Identifier if needed | \* Exterior partition types are named with material composition. Example: If you are unsure, ask or look at what's already in the template and follow that logic. DYNAMO: we have a script that will create walls for each room. #### INTERIOR WALL FINISHES Interior wall finishes that have thickness should be a wall sweep where possible. Using a thin wall is acceptable where a sweep is not applicable but will need to be maintained throughout the project, because if a wall moves the thin wall will not. Locking these thin walls to the main walls is not advised as this slows down the performance of the model. #### MODELING Modeling methodologies depend on the application. Refer to the appendix document outlining some methods for wall modeling. ### CEILINGS All ceilings should be drawn to the inside face of walls. Use caution with auto sketch ceilings. This often puts ceilings in the walls and can create more work with building sections, wall sections, and detail sections. Lights, Registers, Sprinklers, Tech etc. should all be modeled in the Architectural model(s) for location and the Consultants models for quantity. If it matters, model it. Unique special/high profile spaces will need it documented. Typical spaces can be modeled once and then referenced as typical, so mass changes are not needed. NOTE: Reference the appendix document Ceilings.pdf for more information on modeling ceilings. ### MATERIALS The texture files (photos, normal map, bump, etc.) for materials used in any project should be saved in either the Pfluger Master Materials Library or the Temporary Project Textures Library on the Shared Resources Drive (exact file path can be found on the Pfluger Intranet). Naming Convention: Division#_Material_Color_Manufacturer_Applications_SizeInches Example: 04_Brick_Acme_Cocoa-221_Soldier_x32 ### DOORS Pfluger's door families are nested and the Shared Panel Type parameter is driven by the name of the panel family. If you are not an experienced modeler, please seek the help of someone who is, as the door family is complex. #### CURTAIN WALL DOOR: - Method 1: use the curtain walls door family (denoted with a CW in the family name). These families have no frame since the frame is the curtain wall mullion. To draw a door in a curtain wall, change the curtain wall panel to a Wall Type (rather than a panel family) and place the door in that wall as you would normally place a door in a wall. - Method 2: Use the panel door family. Note: you will need to keep an extra eye on your door schedule, so you don't have fractional inches for your panel values. Third Party door hardware plug-ins: Consult your Design Technology Committee member for best practices. ### DATUMS #### GRID LINES - North/ South Grids should be NUMERIC - East/ West Grids should be ALPHA #### LEVELS - NAMING: Level 01, Level 02, etc - PRACTICE: - Levels within Revit should only be made when there are many elements that need that level to change them (i.e. finish floors and roofs are most common), items like Top of Steel or Bottom of deck should only be used when fall within this. You should also utilize the "Building Story" parameter within the level family to be able to have these levels that you may not want to show up in certain views be quickly filtered out. - Where you just need to note the elevation in sections/elevations, use Spot Elevations (located under the annotation tab). Creating levels too close to one another can cause graphical issues. - NEVER DELETE A LEVEL unless you confirm by running a multicategory schedule that nothing is hosted to it. ### ANNOTATION #### TEXT - **ANNOTATION TEXT** - Text should always be capitalized - DYNAMO: we have a script that will - change most displayed text from lowercase to upper case to help management of these - tag all walls (omitting the walls without type marks) with the separate symbols for curtain walls - All annotation text should be Text Type Arial Narrow - Color is typically black, but can vary - Leader type is typically Arrow Filled 15 degrees, but can vary - Family Naming: FontSize FontType (Background)_COLOR_Leader - Example: 3/32" Arial (T) - Background: O=Opaque, T=Transparent - Color and Leader: when different from Pfluger's typical: - Example 1/4" Arial (O)_RED_ClosedCircle - **MODEL TEXT** - Family Naming: MODEL TEXT_Purpose Size - Example: MODEL_Signage 1" #### DIMENSION STYLES - NAMING: DimensionType â€“ FontSize FontType (Background) UnitType - Example: Linear â€“ 3/32" Arial Narrow (O) Inches 1/8" - DIMENSION TYPE: Aligned, Linear, Angular, Radial, Diameter, or Arc. - FONT SIZE: Our standard is 3/32" - FONT TYPE: Our standard is Arial Narrow - BACKGROUND: O=Opaque, T=Transparent - UNITS: Either Project Units or the units chosen if different than that (i.e. inches, feet, etc.) #### LINE STYLES - NAMING: LineWeight # - DescriptorOfPattern - Color - EXAMPLE: 1 - Dashed 1/16" - DrkGrey - STANDARD REVIT TYPES: these line styles will remain to ensure cross collaboration with default Revit families. This includes; Hidden Lines, Insulation Batting Lines, Lines, Medium Lines, Thin Lines, Wide Lines #### KEYNOTING Pfluger's standard for noting contract documents is the Keynote function in Revit. **TYPES OF KEYNOTES AND WHEN TO USE THEM** - Element Keynote - Entire Wall/Floor/Ceiling assemblies - Structural Elements - Family Objects - Material Keynote - Materials within a wall/floor/ceiling assembly. (ie. 5/8" gypsum wall board, 4" metal studs @ 18" O.C) - Finish materials assigned to floor/wall/ceiling assemblies "finish" layer. Ensure all Keynotes are placed in all capital letters. When adding keynotes, one should follow the division to which they relate. For Example: Keynotes added related to various tile flooring elements should remain within the DIVISION 09 or 09 keynote section. Use of the keynote manager application within Revit is highly encouraged for accurate keynoting on projects. NOTE: Ref Pfluger YouTube Channel for a walkthrough on how to use Keynote Manager. ### PHASES AND PHASE FILTERS #### PHASES - The Pfluger template contains Existing and New Construction. - Future phase may be added. When naming, try to be as descriptive as possible. - DO NOT use demo as a phase. In Revit demolish is an action. If elements need to be demolished, they should be demolished in the corresponding phase. - Rooms cannot show up in multiple phases. To get around this you may need to use text to label existing rooms in a demolition drawing. NOTE: Element's in future phases will not show up in views, however elements can still cause conflicts and graphical "issues" with joining, so weigh this as you are strategizing your modeling method. Phases can be combined with past and future phases. #### PHASE FILTERS AND OVERRIDES Should be set up as follows with the corresponding graphic overrides **PHASE FILTERS:** | Filter Name | New | Existing | Demolished | Temporary | |------------|-----|----------|------------|-----------| | 1. Show All | By Category | Overridden | Overridden | Overridden | | 2. Show Complete | By Category | By Category | Not Displayed | Not Displayed | | 3. Show Demo + New | By Category | Not Displayed | Overridden | Overridden | | 4. Show New | By Category | Not Displayed | Not Displayed | Not Displayed | | 5. Show Previous | Not Displayed | Overridden | Not Displayed | Not Displayed | | 6. Show Previous + Demo | Not Displayed | Overridden | Overridden | Not Displayed | | 7. Show Previous + New | By Category | Overridden | Not Displayed | Not Displayed | **GRAPHIC OVERRIDES:** | Phase Status | Projection/Surface | | Cut | | Halftone | Material | |--------------|-------------------|-----|-----|-----|----------|----------| | | Lines | Patterns | Lines | Patterns | | | | Existing | ------------- | | | | â˜ | Phase - Exist | | Demolished | ------------- | | ------------- | Hidden | â˜ | Phase - Demo | | New | _________ | | | â– â– â– â– â– â–  | â˜ | Phase - New | | Temporary | ................. | | ................. | ///////// | â˜ | Phase - Temporary | ### DESIGN OPTIONS Used to convey Alternate Scope in Projects (not to be confused with Worksets for different options to apply to the same condition). - Typically, Design Options are introduced after the Base Bid Scope is modeled, with modifications to that Scope as needed. - Design Options need to be communicated clearly to consultants so that they can show the correct information in their drawings. Consult with the Project Architect for more information. - Naming Convention: Both sets and options should named to convey their content. Don't solely use "Option 2" instead try "Option 2: Science Lab" - Most sets should have an option that is "empty" and set to primary, so content that is not wanted will show by default. NOTE: Ref Pfluger YouTube Channel for a walkthrough on how to use design options. ### PROJECT UNITS - **LENGTH** - Units: Feet and Fractional Inches - Rounding: to nearest 1/256" - Suppress 0 feet - **AREA** - Units: Square feet - Rounding: 0 decimal places - Unit Symbol: SF - Suppress trailing 0's - **VOLUME** - Units: Cubic feet - Rounding: 2 decimal places - Unit Symbol: CF - Suppress trailing 0's - **ANGLE** - Units: Decimal degrees - Rounding: 2 decimal places - Unit Symbol: âˆ˜ - Suppress trailing 0's - **SLOPE** - Units: Rise/ 12" - Rounding: to the nearest 1/256" - **CURRENCY** - Rounding: 2 decimal places - Unit symbol: $ - Suppress trailing 0's - **MASS DENSITY** - Units: Pounds per cubic foot - Rounding: 2 decimal places - Unit symbol: lb/ftÂ³ - Suppress trailing 0's **IMPORTANT: you MUST model in 1/256" if you model using a rounded dimension, that's not a true dimension. The rounded dimension you see isn't guaranteed to be that dimension. For example, if you round to the nearest Â¼" your element could anywhere within 0"-1/4" There have been instances where this was not adhered to, and it created major issues.** ### LINKING FILES - Linking between Revit Models should be origin to origin. However, this cannot always happen. If linking needs to occur after two models have elements in them, shared coordinates should be used - NOTE: ref appendix document, Tip_Points.pdf - CAD FILES: Only Link. Center to center and then rotated & moved. This is extremely important because the #1 cause of a slow performing model is imported CAD files. - NOTE: ref appendix document, Link_DWG.pdf - DYNAMO: we have a script that will report on how CAD files are inserted into a project (e.g. linked v imported) to help model management - ACC: All linked files (Revit, CAD, etc.) shall be saved to the appropriate folder in the ACC project file and then linked. DO NOT link any content from your local computer or local Teams/Sharepoint Folder. - i. Pfluger Standard it to use the live linking methodology for Revit to Revit Linking. ### DRAWINGS #### DRAWING INDEX Drawing indexes can be formed in two ways - Dummy Data: in the index schedule, you can input rows of data for sheets that are not issued by Pfluger so they appear in our index of drawings. - Link Sheets into Index: this requires coordination with consultants. - NOTE: Reference the appendix document drawing index.pdf - DYNAMO: we have a script that will create sheets or dummy sheets based on an excel file #### LIFE SAFETY PLANS The Life safety plan shall act as a one-stop reference for the design team, AHJ, and contactor for the code requirements that shaped the design. Information should be limited only to what is needed to convey the code solutions; other extraneous info should be hidden. Special care should be taken to ensure that graphical indications of rating or barrier are legible at the scale presented. Pfluger's life safety plans are heavily dependent on view filters and visibility graphic settings. The filters are dependent on the Fire Rating parameter, ensure that this parameter is filled out and that you are using the Life Safety View Template. In additions to graphics, these elements need to be included/calculated - Legend: should be filled out according to the Life Safety Analysis for your building. - NOTE: reference Pfluger Intranet for video guide on how to perform a Life Safety Analysis. - Fire Cabinets and Extinguishers - Longest path of travel - NOTE: reference the appendix document Revit Longest Path.pdf - Exit width indicators. - Room Tag with occupancy totals - DYNAMO: we have a script that will apply the calculated value of occupants to the parameter in the room tag - Fire Areas - Areas (rated tunnel/corridor, area of refuge, etc.) #### DEMOLITION PLANS Demolition plans should cover all items and assemblies that must be removed to allow new construction to commence. General description tags can be placed per room for large unitary items (e.g., remove carpet). Items that a bidder would need to assign additional value to remove should be individually called out. Demo notes shall be objective and quantitative and shall avoid nebulous unbiddable statements. Descriptions should not creep into new work scope (e.g., patch and paint); follow up in new work scope to cover said items. - Phase & Phase Filtering: the phase of the view should be set to New Construction, and the Phase Filter should be set to Show Previous and Demo. - Demo Keynotes: using an annotation symbol and Note Block, note scope of work - Not all things can be shown using modeling. There may be times where you will need to use detail items to denote items for demo. - Additional drawings: other drawings may need to be used to identify important items for demolition. If it's important, call it out. #### DOOR SCHEDULE - Door schedules should be used to convey styles, height, width and any other unique and relevant identifying information for your project. Use of this space to delineate between emergency egress doors and convenience/security doors is useful. The measurements shown in the door schedule should represent the actual door width. Rough opening sizes need not be shown in the door schedule. When using 3rd party door management software be sure to only import information relevant to your project into the door schedule - When working with existing conditions use of the phase filter within the door schedule will aide in clearly communicating design intent and hardware needs for the projects. DYNAMO: we have the following scripts that will save you IMENSE amounts of time in regard to doors: - Number doors to match room numbers - Export/Import Door HDW Data via excel - Retrieve wall type doors are in (for use with schedule key to autofill HJS details) - Finds doors in walls that are thicker than allowed by ADA ### VIEWS #### WORKING IN VIEWS As you work in the model, it is important to pay attention to how you organize views and the level the view is associated with, for the following key reasons: - Most modeled elements are hosted to levels. # Meaningful Human Experience

## Defined

### Introduction

We believe that whenever collaboration and problem-solving occur, the outcome should be a meaningful human experience (MHE). Our purpose is to inspire people to create a more meaningful human experience, starting with each of us. Whether it's for our clients, partners, or team members, understanding how to craft these experiences is important. Our work should create exceptional buildings and results for our clients while making the process inspiring.

**Producing a meaningful human experience consists of four essential components: structure, engagement, reflection, and discovery.**

## Components of a Meaningful Human Experience

Everyone, regardless of their role, can confidently and seamlessly experience an MHE. But how do you incorporate each of these into a process or a project? First, we must define what each one means to Pfluger.

â€¢ **Structure** â€“ We develop an intentional framework that provides clarity and promotes a shared devotion to finding/creating/discovering something special.

â€¢ **Engagement** â€“We collaborate, inspire, and explore one another's ideas with a curious mindset and an elevated level of trust.

â€¢ **Reflection** â€“ We step away to decompress and create opportunities to cultivate new perspectives.

â€¢ **Discovery** â€“ We are curious problem seekers, continuously learning by asking probing questions, challenging assumptions, and exploring multiple perspectives to achieve innovative solutions.

## Implementing These Components

Now that we have defined the components, we need to understand how they can be integrated into our process and our projects. Here are some examples that demonstrate how you can integrate a MHE into your daily work:

### Structure

â€¢ **Meeting Design:** Design a meeting where participants understand the purpose, process, and payoff. Curate an agenda that includes opportunities for engagement, reflection and discovery. We have a database of multiple meeting designs used with clients to inspire them as we understand their vision and guiding principles.

â€¢ **Standardized Documents and Checklists:** Pfluger has a robust set of standards for our projects and has developed a checklist for each phase. These ensure firm-wide consistency and thoroughness, allowing us to leverage staff from multiple offices to contribute meaningfully to a project at any phase.

â€¢ **Workspace:** Our workspaces offer versatility through technology, furniture, and various room types. This structure allows us to focus on our creative work. Open areas encourage collaboration, movement, and expansive thinking. Smaller rooms provide spaces for quiet reflection.

### Engagement

â€¢ **Project Success**
    - a. External: Visioning Process: We are intentional about how we engage with each client during our visioning workshops to create a community of stakeholders deeply invested in the project's success. Our activities, while thought-provoking, future-focused, and collaborative, are customized to each client's needs and expectations. This community of stakeholders remains active in shaping the project's vision.
    - b. Internal: Pin-Ups: Our weekly pin-ups engage with all staff, regardless of role, to collaborate on a particular design challenge. These are not structured to be a report-out of a project but instead to encourage curiosity and problem-solving. By bringing together different perspectives, we expand the range of ideas and possibilities, creating the opportunity for both practical and innovative solutions.

â€¢ **Business Development:** We build our business by creating strong, trust-based client relationships. We do this by developing meaningful strategies to connect with key leaders. We attend board meetings to understand the dynamics of the organization and each member. We go on tours with key stakeholders to gather insight on likes and dislikes. We sit down with decision-makers to understand their challenges and demonstrate our commitment to help solve them. We stay in tune with our clients at regular intervals throughout all phases of our work by sharing a meal together and delivering face-to-face client satisfaction surveys.

### Reflection

â€¢ **Cognitive Breaks:** How often have you been sitting in traffic and suddenly thought of a way to solve that pesky problem eating at you? Stepping away from the problem and doing an unrelated task allows your mind to relax. Examples of these breaks include exercising, being in nature, driving without the "radio" on, refilling your coffee or tea, or even sleeping on it. Intentionally giving yourself time away will mitigate mental fatigue and foster creative thinking.
    - a. External: We do not want to do charrettes or stack meetings; need to build breaks between meetings to allow for everyone to decompress and reflect on the design

â€¢ **Internal Team Debrief:** Reflecting after a meeting or engagement on what the group liked, lacked, learned, and longed for creates an intentional reflection that makes our future work better. After a milestone project meeting, the PM, PA, and PD compare notes and discuss any action item that needs to be disseminated to the rest of the project team. This small group provides a chance to bounce ideas off each other and formulate a game plan for follow-up to-dos.

**Reflective Prompts:** Thoughtful questions can provoke thinking far beyond the moment and can 'stick with us' for days on end as we continue to process. Examples of reflective prompts are included below and are utilized in internal and external meetings.

Examples from a client visioning process:
- "If rooms are boxes, what would happen if the boxes were gone?"
- "In what unexpected places do we find educational settings?"

Examples from an internal leadership team retreat:

    - o What work should we eliminate that no longer serves our goals?
    - o What work could you delegate that would provide a learning opportunity for others on our team?

### Discovery

â€¢ **Workshops/Retreats:** We intentionally design sessions to provide moments of discovery among attendees. Through small group discussions with open-ended questions or creative tasks, participants are free to explore various possibilities.
    - **External:** Pfluger Architects' discovery process with Midland ISD high schools exemplifies our goal to inspire and create meaningful human experiences. We started with our Breaking of the Bread, sitting alongside district leadership, asking future-focused questions, and listening intently to form a collaborative team. Our process included an activity, Postcards from the Future, and a customized visioning game, Form + Function. These multi-dimensional activities helped stakeholders identify and reflect on key experiences they envision at the new campuses, leading to an understanding of the types of spaces that can be designed to support them.

We took a cognitive break over dinner and reconvened as a smaller group to reflect and evaluate. This smaller group made several discoveries by challenging each other's ideas and working to find common ground.

â€¢ **Survey:** Using a survey can be a strategy for producing moments of discovery for the one surveying and the individuals being surveyed. Surveys can create moments of pause and reflection to gain critical insights that can help shape how best to engage a stakeholder group, tap into diverse perspectives, look for common themes, and so much more. ## Measuring the Meaningful Human Experience

Now that we have defined the components of a meaningful human experience, we need to understand how the experience is measured. We believe that if we design client and staff experiences to generate meaningful human experiences, the result is a number of Aha! Moments, pleasant and unexpected experiences, ideas, or breakthroughs. We aspire to create these Aha! Moments, planned and unplanned, in every structured opportunity involving collaboration and problem-solving. We prioritize quality over quantity, where a collective group experiences the same Aha!

â€¢ **Aha!** â€“ When we create an Aha! Moment, our clients, team members, and/or partners have a pleasant and unexpected experience, idea, or breakthrough that comes from each of the components. We anticipate that every meaningful human experience will yield more than one Aha! during the overall process. We want everyone who engages with this process to have these enlightenments that inspire us to go above and beyond a simple task/assignment.

### Aha! Examples:

#### Midland ISD Payback Analysis

During our interview with Midland ISD, we noted that funds generated using bond proceeds can be used to reduce Maintenance & Operations costs, thereby allowing money to be redirected to the classroom. We suggested that IF this is important to the district, they could use bond proceeds or related interest earnings to purchase solar arrays on the new high schools that could greatly reduce or even eliminate the cost of energy for these schools to operate. This suggestion offered value that wasn't anticipated, which resulted in Pfluger developing a detailed payback analysis for the district's consideration.

#### Contract Administration Training

We believe that meaningful experiences include structure. The Contract Administration workshop in mid-spring of 2024 was a great example of this. We designed the workshop not just to share Pfluger Standards for executing contract administration but also to build stronger relationships between individuals in different offices. The goal was to foster a sense that we're all working together, even if we're not in the same place.

We kicked things off with an icebreaker that had nothing to do with contract administration but helped everyone loosen up and get to know each other better. This set a positive tone for the rest of the workshop. The presentations were the result of months of planning and collaboration. We worked through the details of each topic and developed a consensus among the most experienced and senior people from each office. By the time the presentations were happening, we were all on the same page.

We also included several open-ended topics to encourage conversation and brainstorming about possible improvements to our system. In between presentations, participants engaged in group work and breakout projects, which helped break up the monotony of sitting and listening to lectures.

While we didn't categorize all the "Aha!" moments during the workshop, one realization that slowly dawned on everyone during the planning and implementation was that we actually do have CA standards we can agree on across the firm. Initially, this seemed questionable since each office thought their way of doing things was slightly different from the others. Participants had opportunities to make better connections and learned that we have standards. They saw the effort and value provided.

### Measuring Aha!

â€¢ **External Measurement:**
    - o Incorporate how to measure Aha! into our current design process. (Working with Christian on this.)

â€¢ **Internal Measurement:**
    - o When we are working to deliver an MHE internally, integrate opportunities for team members to reflect on the Aha! Moments they had and share them with the team. Individuals responsible for managing the project and/or leading the initiative are responsible for bringing reflection and discussion to the group.
    - o All employees can reflect on Aha! Moments throughout their work and career at Pfluger. Everyone is encouraged to keep track of their Aha! Moments and share with their team lead/manager.

## Final Thoughts

A Meaningful Human Experience is personal. We cannot mass-produce an MHE, nor is that our goal. Instead, our job is to do our best to thoughtfully craft opportunities for people to experience their own meaning.

**For Clients:** Confident, solutions-focused, and respectful of their goals. We highlight expertise without overstating results.

**For Consultants:** Direct and collaborative. We ensure clarity and mutual respect and understanding.

**For the Community:** Inclusive and approachable, focusing on positive impact.

**For Internal Teams:** Motivating and goal-focused, fostering teamwork and open dialogue.

#### ADJUSTING TONE FOR FORMAL SITUATIONS

Some situations call for a formal approach. When communicating with regulatory bodies or submitting official reports, we use a respectful, precise tone. Avoid contractions and casual phrases. Be concise but thorough. Example:

âœ˜ The project is being aligned in a manner that rigorously adheres to state regulatory frameworks and is structured to fulfill all requisite compliance obligations.

âœ” The project aligns with state regulations and meets all necessary compliance standards.

---

### Our Style

Our style is rooted in simplicity, clarity, and purpose. We use the ISO Plain Language Model to make our writing easy to read and understand.

**Use Active Voice:** Keep sentences engaging and direct. For example:

âœ˜ The building was designed to maximize natural light.

âœ˜ Compliance with state regulations was ensured by the team.

âœ” We designed the building to maximize natural light.

âœ” The team ensured compliance with state regulations.

**Make it Flow:** Every sentence should connect logically to the next. Example: after mentioning a project's design, discuss how that design solves a problem or meets a need.

**Keep It Simple:** Use clear, straightforward words. For example, say "consider" instead of "give consideration to," and "use" rather than "utilize." Write with the words you would say, not the words you'd use to convince your professor you know what you're talking about. Eschew the obfuscation of information!

**Use the Inverted Pyramid Method:** Put the most important information first. If people only read the first sentence, what should they take away? For example, if you were writing something for a community paper to get support for a project:

âœ˜ A new school will serve 800 students and include energy-efficient systems, flexible classrooms, and outdoor learning spaces. The project is expected to take 18 months to complete and will address the district's growing enrollment demands. To fund the project, the district has proposed a $50 million budget.

âœ” The district has proposed a $50 million budget for a new elementary school to address growing enrollment demands. Planned to serve 800 students, the school will feature energy-efficient systems, flexible classrooms, and outdoor learning spaces. If approved, the project is expected to take 18 months to complete.

---

### Grammar and Punctuation

#### AP Stylebook

Follow the AP Stylebook, (password is in Keeper), which prioritizes punctuation and grammar for clarity and understanding. Our one exception to the AP Stylebook is the Oxford comma, which we use for clarity in lists. Example:

âœ˜ We invited the teachers, John and Jane to the meeting. (This could imply that John and Jane are the teachers.)

âœ” We invited the teachers, John, and Jane to the meeting.

#### Capitalization

The AP Stylebook generally minimizes capitalization. Use capital letters for proper nouns, formal titles before names, and specific entities (like organizations, committees, and official documents).

**Committees:** Capitalize the full names of specific committees. Do not capitalize generic references.

"The MISD Steering Committee for the new school project met to discuss the design." Generic: "The steering committee met to discuss the project's progress."

**Titles:** Capitalize titles when they come before a name. Do not capitalize titles when they follow a name or are used in a general sense.

Specific: "Managing Principal, Jane Doe led the project." Generic: "Jane Doe, the managing principal, led the project."

**Document Titles:** Capitalize the full titles of specific documents. When referring to documents in general, do not capitalize unless it starts a sentence.

Specific: "The MISD 2024 Annual Report provides detailed financial information." Generic: "The annual report will be released in January."

#### Bulleted Lists

**Capitalization and Punctuation in Bulleted Lists:**

Full sentences: Begin with a capital letter and end with appropriate punctuation. Example:
- We prioritize active voice in our writing.
- Our tone is always professional and approachable.

Phrases or fragments: Start with a lowercase letter unless the word is a proper noun or typically capitalized. These items do not need punctuation unless needed for clarity. Example (key project features):
- cost efficiency
- community involvement
- preservation of historical elements

If you have a mix of full sentences and fragments, try to rewrite the list for consistency. If that's not possible, maintain clear communication even if punctuation varies.

## Terms & Abbreviations

### TERMS

**Activities:** Business development touchpoints and interactions.

**Basic Consultant:** see Direct Consultant

**Billable:** Time and expenses that can be charged directly to a client outside of a lumpsum or % construction contract. This is typically what is used in a T&E project.

**Charge Type:** A classification system in Vantagepoint that distinguishes between overhead and billable projects (known as regular).

**CRM:** Client Relationship Management. A system designed to manage the firm's interactions with current and potential clients.

**Direct Consultant:** (Basic Consultant) The consultant fee is deducted from our fee. This is typically our basic service consultants like MEP, Structural, and Civil.

**Direct Hours/Labor:** The time spent by employees working directly on production or delivery for a billable project.

**ERP:** Enterprise Resource Planning. A software system that helps the firm streamline core business processes â€“ including project management, time tracking, resource planning, finance, and business development â€“ with a unified view of activity. It serves as a single source of truth to guide data-driven decision making.

**Estimate-at-Complete (EAC):** The total projected value at project completion, based on actuals to date and future forecasts. Used for hours, revenue, billing, cost, etc.

**Estimate-to-Complete (ETC):** The projected remaining value needed from now until project completion. Used for hours, revenue, billing, cost, etc.

**Fields:** Areas in Vantagepoint where you can enter or store data.

**Grids:** Multiple fields arranged in a table view.

**Hub:** An area in Vantagepoint used to manage information about projects, clients, vendors, and employees. Located vertically on the left-hand side of the system.

**In-Pursuit:** Projects that are in the firm's pipeline.

**Indirect Hours/Labor:** The time spent by employees on tasks that support the overall operations of the firm but aren't tied to a specific billable project.

**Job to Date (JTD):** The actual amounts recorded to date for a project. Used for hours, revenue, billing, cost, etc.

**Net Revenue:** Gross Revenue â€“ Non-Labor Costs (consultants, reimbursables, etc.).

**Net Revenue Multiplier:** A ratio of Net Revenue divided by Direct Labor.

**Non-Billable:** Time and expenses that cannot be charged to the client, either because it's already included in the fee (lumpsum or % construction) or because it falls outside the project scope.

**Period:** A defined time frame used for finance and reporting purposes. Typically, one calendar month.

**Pinnacle Membership:** A recognition and leadership track for individuals who make significant contributions to the firm and the profession. Structured in three tiers, each reflecting increasing levels of impact: Associate, Senior Associate, and Principal.

**Pipeline:** The process of tracking potential projects from early business development to contract award. It tracks the stage and likelihood of winning each project as it progresses.

**Phase:** Second level of the work breakdown structure in Vantagepoint

**Reimbursable:** Project-related expenses that are outlined in the contract and can be charged back to the client as they occur.

**Reimbursable Consultant:** The consultant fee is in addition to our fee. This is typically our supplemental and additional service consultants like roofing, food service, and acoustics.

**Smart Search:** Searches that suggests a value based on a few characters entered.

**Stage:** Various milestones within the project pipeline.

**Supplemental Consultants:** see Reimbursable Consultant

**Tab:** Each hub has a standard set of tabs to help organize data for the selected record. Located horizontally along the top of the system.

**Task:** Third and lowest level of the work breakdown structure in Vantagepoint

**WBS:** Work Breakdown Structure. A hierarchical breakdown of a project into smaller, manageable components (phases, tasks, etc.) that are tied together in a tree structure.

## Timesheet & Absence Requests Policies

### Timesheets

#### Timesheet Deadlines

- The timesheet week begins on Saturday and ends on Friday.
- Timesheets must be submitted every **Friday by 11:59PM.**
- People Leaders & Project Managers must review timesheets and coordinate any necessary adjustments with employees by **Monday at 11:59PM.**
- Timesheets lock Tuesday morning as payroll processing begins.

#### Timesheet Corrections After Lock

If a correction is needed after Tuesday, employees must make the adjustment on their next timesheet by performing an "in-and-out" entry. An "in-and-out" entry includes marking negative hours on the miscoded item (project, phase, or task) and positive hours on the correct item.

#### Chain of Escalation

**If you don't know where to log time, don't guess.** Use the appropriate chain of escalation path:
- Overhead Time: Employee > People Leaders > People & Culture
- Project Time: Employee > Project Manager > Finance

# SECTION 1: VISION & FRAMEWORK

## 1.1 Vision Statement

The application of architectural research into built works assisted by computational intelligence.

## 1.2 Core Principles

### 1.2.1 The Why: Alignment with Pfluger Core Values

Research and benchmarking is a way to live out the Pfluger core values: Do What's Right, Build Synergy, Make a Difference, and Never Settle. When these are used to focus on problems, novel solutions can occur, discovering the 'What's Next'.

The R&B Framework exists to aid in the research process, so you can enjoy the creative exploration without getting tied up in the busy work. Novel research isn't just seen as a marketing strategy; it can serve as a creative outlet for architecture that isn't on a project.

While escaping to Mars sounds great, a focus of the Pfluger R&B is to link it back to our work under the focus of Experiential Learning and how we can use this new knowledge to better our built environment.

The R&B department operates on the principle that research should directly inform practice. By systematically investigating questions related to experiential learning environments, Pfluger positions itself to lead rather than follow industry trends. This approach serves multiple purposes: it creates competitive advantage in project pursuits, develops internal expertise that elevates design quality, provides professional development opportunities for staff, and generates publishable thought leadership that raises firm visibility.

Research at Pfluger is not an academic exercise disconnected from delivery. Every research initiative is tied to either an active project where findings can be immediately applied, or a strategic area where future projects are anticipated. This ensures research investment yields tangible returns in built work quality and client value.

### 1.2.2 The Focus: Experiential Learning in Educational Architecture

As architectural trends constantly shift across all sectors, the current objective is the evolving philosophy of experiential learning. This can be divided into many topics and subcategories, but it revolves around the experience of education rather than memorization.

While the educational pedagogy is on the educator's side, the physical space is the special stage that the architect can curate. With a new flexible pedagogy comes the possibility of rethinking the physical armature of educational spaces.

Key questions:
- Are there new tools at our disposal?
- Are there new tools that will need new spaces?
- How can the digital be synchronized with the physical?

Experiential learning represents a fundamental shift from passive knowledge absorption to active engagement. Students learn by doing, experimenting, collaborating, and reflecting rather than sitting in rows absorbing lectures. This pedagogical evolution demands architectural response.

The R&B focus examines how physical environments can support diverse learning modalities: hands-on making spaces, flexible collaboration zones, quiet reflection areas, technology-rich immersive environments, and spaces that blur indoor/outdoor boundaries. Research investigates what spatial qualities, material choices, lighting conditions, acoustic properties, and technological integrations best support different types of experiential learning activities.

This focus extends beyond K-12 into higher education, career technical education, and lifelong learning environments. By building a knowledge base around experiential learning spaces, Pfluger develops expertise that differentiates the firm in educational sector pursuits and elevates design outcomes across all education project types.

### 1.2.3 Strategic Use of AI

There are many AI tools. As an old saying goes, 'with great power comes great responsibility'. The capacity of ChatGPT 4 greatly surpasses the common knowledge of a layperson and architects, while specialized individuals can not compete with the knowledge set.

This is important to remember as while AI can do a lot, know a lot, and say a lot, we are behind the curve, and must not assume correctness. Steps and measures have been taken to isolate the level of AI creativity in the Pfluger Agents. However, the technology is not currently perfect.

Pfluger has outlined a series of AI best practices allowing us to explore these new tools without compromising our values and obligations.

AI represents a paradigm shift in architectural communication - moving beyond traditional 2D plan-based communication methods to new forms of spatial understanding and documentation.

The R&B department utilizes Claude AI as the primary computational intelligence tool with 5 dedicated research accounts (research1@pflugerarchitects.com through research5@pflugerarchitects.com). This AI infrastructure accelerates research workflows by: assisting with literature review and source synthesis, helping formulate research questions and hypotheses, analyzing survey data and identifying patterns, drafting research documentation and reports, and maintaining version control through GitHub integration.

AI usage is tracked as a key performance metric. The department measures both AI utilization rates and resulting work output to quantify time savings and productivity gains. This data-driven approach ensures AI tools deliver measurable value while maintaining quality standards. All AI-assisted work follows established best practices to ensure accuracy, proper attribution, and alignment with firm values. The goal is not to replace human expertise but to amplify researcher capacity, allowing deeper investigation and higher quality outputs within constrained time budgets.

### 1.2.4 User Experience Philosophy

Research can be a different way of thinking compared to a typical creative mindset. It involves the objective rather than the artistic subjective.

To assist in this jump, a series of templates, forms, connections, and AI tools have been curated to assist in the research journey. A common take on using tools to advance efficiency is that there is now additional leftover time to do more. It is essential to see the forest through the trees on this; these tools should be used to create time to explore further and advance, rather than do less in a bulk response.

Time and budget allotments have also been curated to respect the ongoing work and projects and balance research undertakings. With the recent abundance and progress of artificial intelligence in architecture, from image generators to Chat GPT, it is an R&B focus to steer towards these tools rather than away from them and embrace the newfound abilities to do better and take on more meaningful work.

The R&B framework provides structured support throughout the research journey. Each researcher receives a personal claude.md configuration file that captures their research focus, ongoing projects, preferred working methods, and individual context. This personalized AI configuration ensures consistent, contextually-aware assistance across research sessions.

Standardized templates guide pitch development, hypothesis formation, methodology selection, and deliverable preparation. The GreenLight Team provides active support in refining research questions, identifying partners, and navigating approval processes. Time tracking through project-specific billing codes (T01-xx series) ensures research effort is visible and valued. Touchpoint schedules appropriate to research scope (Simple/Medium/Complex) provide structure without micromanagement. This infrastructure removes administrative friction, allowing researchers to focus cognitive energy on substantive investigation rather than process navigation.

### 1.2.5 User Analytics & Continuous Improvement

Modern technology uses its users' analytics to charge advancements, directly to and indirectly to its own technology. Pfluger uses analytics in the same way to outline inefficiencies in the process and create improvement targets.

For internal AI applications, Pfluger collects bulk conversions, resource utilization, and activity to see what is used most often and how it is used. This type of feedback allows for streamlined updates and improvements to the various tools.

While this objective data can be aggregated in mass, subjective data is gathered via a survey of the tools. It is vital to complete these in any capacity to target areas for advancement accurately. Occasionally, an AI agent may reach out or collect information during a conversation about an issue it cannot assist with.

The R&B department tracks two primary metric categories: AI utilization and research output. AI utilization metrics include frequency of Claude usage per researcher, types of tasks supported by AI, time spent in AI-assisted vs. unassisted work, and GitHub commit activity showing AI-supported documentation. Research output metrics include number of research projects initiated and completed, hours invested per deliverable type, publication and presentation outcomes, and integration instances where research influenced project design decisions.

By comparing AI utilization against output metrics, the department quantifies time savings and productivity gains. This analysis informs resource allocation decisions, identifies where AI tools provide maximum value, reveals process bottlenecks requiring attention, and demonstrates ROI on AI infrastructure investment. Regular analysis cycles (quarterly) ensure the framework evolves based on measured performance rather than assumptions.

### 1.2.6 Impact & Analysis

The impact of research can range from immediate to long-term, and the impact can be proportional to the time taken to complete the research. The North Star impact of conducting research at Pfluger is to integrate 'What's Next' into our built environment via our work.

Research impact manifests across multiple timescales and domains. Immediate impact occurs when research findings directly inform active project design decisions, improving outcomes for current clients. Short-term impact appears in successful project pursuits where demonstrated research expertise differentiates Pfluger from competitors. Medium-term impact builds as published research and conference presentations establish firm thought leadership, attracting clients seeking innovation. Long-term impact accumulates as repeated research cycles build deep institutional knowledge in experiential learning environments, positioning Pfluger as the recognized expert in this domain.

Impact assessment tracks both quantitative measures (projects won, publications produced, citations received, design awards earned) and qualitative measures (client feedback, peer recognition, staff professional development). Each research project includes an impact plan identifying how findings will be applied, disseminated, and measured. This ensures research investment generates tangible returns rather than producing reports that sit unused on digital shelves.

### 1.2.7 Process Limitations & Assumptions

The intent of research at Pfluger is to enhance our work and its impact on the end user. While these effects can be translated to other sectors and areas, such as urban planning, assumptions allow research some flexibility by defining a safe and exploratory environment.

**Key Assumptions & Limitations:**

1. All Pfluger research must be GreenLit before commencing/Sponsored.

2. All employees can research intricate topics with the assistance of a Pfluger Partner.

3. If there is no active project to incorporate research into, a fictitious project can be created.

4. Research must be architecturally focused on experiential learning.

5. Research completion can not negatively influence employee standing.

6. The researcher must facilitate the coordination between the researcher and their respective project team.

## 2.1 Research Process Overview

### 2.1.1 Call for Pitches Process

The research process starts with a call for pitches. With the focus of Experiential Learning, researchers submit pitches through The Repository (repository.pflugerarchitects.com), either selecting a pre-approved GreenLit topic or pitching their own idea with Ezra AI guidance (see Section 3.2.4).

**Supplied Gaps**: Strategically picked in alignment with current or coming online projects and have identified research partners.

**Open Exploration**: Allows the applicant to explore a gap that may not immediately apply to a project.

For all pitches, it is up to the research applicant to derive a research idea and a research method. The GreenLight Team can assist with optional aspects such as:
- Timeline
- Funding
- Resources
- Research partners

As funding and research partnerships can be nebulous, they can be identified more in-depth during the submission process. Still, they must have an identified boundary, such as 'needed travel to a school for a survey', 'a superintendent to interview', etc.

### 2.1.2 Research Development Stages

Research work is tracked through distinct phases:

**Pre-Research (040)**: Background material gathering, literature reviews, precedent studies, or other preparatory content before formal research begins. Active during small/medium/large-scale research efforts (S/M/L).

**Schematic Research (050)**: Early development of research content - forming hypotheses, outlining structure, or initiating pilot experiments. Active during large-scale research efforts (L).

**Developmental Research (060)**: Formalizing and refining research content. Active during small/medium/large-scale research efforts (S/M/L).

**Final Research (070)**: Time spent preparing final deliverables, including polished writeups, graphics, documentation, publication-ready materials, and SharePoint page creation.

**Presentation Research (080)**: Work related to creating specific presentation materials (e.g., PowerPoint decks) for internal sharing, public events, or external partners. Active for medium and large projects.

**Research Project Integration (090)**: When research is integrated into an architectural project. Time should be billed to the project number, with a comment referencing the related RBxx code (e.g., "See X25_RB03").

## 2.2 Research Question Development

### 2.2.1 Formulating the Research Question

Formulate a specific, measurable, focused research question on an idea that frames your investigation's central issue (e.g., "How does X affect Y?"). Ensure the research question is specific, measurable, and focused. If your guiding question is vague, you may need to refine it further to make it more precise.

### 2.2.2 Identifying Variables

**Independent Variable (X)**: The variable you suspect influences the outcome.

**Dependent Variable (Y)**: This variable changes due to the influence of the independent variable.

### 2.2.3 Hypothesis Development

Present a testable prediction that outlines the expected relationship between the independent and dependent variables.

**Null Hypothesis (H0)**: This suggests no relationship between the independent and dependent variables. It represents the default position that your research will attempt to disprove.

**Alternative Hypothesis (H1)**: This suggests a relationship between the independent and dependent variables. It represents the hypothesis you will test and potentially support.

### 2.2.4 Making the Hypothesis Testable

Ensure the hypothesis is measurable and can be evaluated using research methods like surveys, experiments, or statistical analysis.

**Measurable variable**: Time spent on social media (measured in hours per day).

**Measurable outcome**: Academic performance (measured by GPA or test scores).

### 2.2.5 Ensuring Clarity and Specificity

Clearly indicate the expected relationship, specifying conditions or thresholds if necessary (e.g., "students who spend more than 3 hours a day on social media have lower GPAs").

**Clear**: "The more time a student spends on social media, the lower their GPA will be."

**Specific**: Instead of just saying "more time," specify the threshold (e.g., "students who spend more than 3 hours a day on social media").

**Testable**: Ensure you can measure the variables in your study (e.g., measuring time on social media in hours and GPA on a numerical scale).

### 2.2.6 Implications & Literature Review

**Consider the Implications**: Consider how the results of your study could influence real-world outcomes, such as improving educational strategies or informing policy.

**Literature Review**: Conduct a literature review to understand prior findings and refine the hypothesis, ensuring it builds on existing knowledge or addresses identified gaps.

## 2.4 Research Methodology Framework

### 2.4.1 Research Design Approaches

Define the overall framework of the study to understand what your data will be:

**Literature Review/Analysis**: Focusing on existing research to discuss/identify an interesting gap

**Quantitative Data**: Use charts, graphs, and statistics to identify patterns, trends, and relationships

**Qualitative Data**: Sort responses into themes or categories to find common ideas and insights

**Mixed Methods**: Combine numbers (charts and graphs) with written summaries to give a full picture of the findings

### 2.4.2 Data Collection Methods

Describe the methods used to gather the data, including how many participants or sources will be involved. Common methods include:

**Surveys and Questionnaires**: Asking a group of people the same set of questions

**Interviews**: Speaking with individuals to get detailed answers (structured, semi-structured, or unstructured)

**Observations**: Watching and recording behaviors or interactions

**Experiments**: Testing ideas in a controlled setting to see what happens

**Document or Content Analysis**: Reviewing written materials, images, or other media for patterns and insights

### 2.4.3 Data Analysis Strategies

Explain how the collected information will be organized and understood:

**Statistical Analysis**: Using numbers, charts, and graphs to find patterns in data

**Thematic Analysis**: Sorting written or spoken responses into common themes or ideas

**Content Analysis**: Examining documents, images, or media to identify key topics or trends

### 2.4.4 Ethical Considerations

Discusses any ethical concerns related to the research:

**Protecting confidentiality**: Keeping participant information private and secure

**Obtaining consent**: Making sure participants understand the study and agree to take part

**Minimizing harm**: Avoiding risks or negative impacts on participants

**Using NDAs (if needed)**: Protecting sensitive information with non-disclosure agreements

### 2.4.5 Limitations Documentation

Describe any limitations and factors that could impact the study's accuracy or scope:

**Known biases**: Business relationships, personal perspectives, or market influence that may affect findings

**Sample size constraints**: Limitations due to the number of participants or available data

**External factors**: Uncontrollable elements like economic shifts, policy changes, or environmental conditions that might influence results

### 2.4.6 Research Connections & Partners

Identify key players or contacts that can be leveraged to assist in the research topic. These can include regulatory bodies or companies.

**Tracking Template:**
- Organization/Affiliation
- Name
- Contact
- Relevance/Involvement
- Date Contacted
- Future Potential

### 2.4.7 Literature Review Methodology

**Choosing the Right Sources**
- Identify 3-4 peer-reviewed articles, books, or authoritative reports that have contributed to the field you're researching
- Provide insight into the independent and dependent variables in your research question

**Summarizing the Insight**
- To build your argument and hypothesis, summarize the source's insight into your understanding of the relationship between your variables

**Identify The Gaps or Contradictions**
- To help justify your research, identify what is missing or underexplored in existing studies that your research might address with further investigation

**Hypothesis Connection**
- To show that your hypothesis is a reasoned prediction, explain how the literature review findings lead you to the developed hypothesis

**APA Citations and Reference List**
- Use APA citations to give credit to the authors of the sources you are referencing

## 2.5 Conclusion & Insights Framework

### 2.5.1 Hypothesis Evaluation

**Was the hypothesis supported?**

- Reiterate the primary claim or hypothesis you were testing in your study
- Briefly highlight the most significant insights of the study and how they contribute to understanding the research question or hypothesis. Were the findings in line with what you expected?
- Reference specific data or outcomes from your research that provide evidence to support or challenge the hypothesis
- If the findings were different from what you anticipated, explain these deviations and provide potential reasons why

### 2.5.2 Continuing Research Opportunities

Reflect on limitations or unanswered questions in your study and propose directions for future research:

**Broader Sample**: If your study had a small sample size or if it was limited to a particular group, suggest a broader or more diverse sample

**Longitudinal Studies**: If your research was cross-sectional (a snapshot at one point in time), suggest that longitudinal studies (which track participants over time) could provide deeper insights into how changes occur

**Methodology Improvements**: Propose improvements to the methodology, such as refining data collection methods, using new technological tools, or adding qualitative components (like interviews or focus groups) to complement the quantitative findings

**Interdisciplinary Integration**: Suggest an interdisciplinary perspective where your research could be integrated with other fields of study

# SECTION 4: AI TOOLS & BEST PRACTICES

## 4.1 AI Best Practices

### 4.1.1 Philosophy

For Safe, Creative, and Responsible Integration of AI into Pfluger's Workflows.

The intent of the best practices is to include a safety net for the usage of AI in the architectural process without hindering its ability to assist in various aspects. A central premise is that AI should be used to create time to focus on enhancing the priority, not to create time to enhance other priorities.

The best practices will be used alongside the firm's Approved AI Tools List and Keeper credentials.

### 4.1.2 DOs

**1. Use approved AI tools**
- Reference the alternative AI tools list
- Example: You enhance a render in Krea using your firm Keeper login
- Access logins via Keeper using company-wide accounts
- If a tool isn't listed, submit a request via the Alternative AI Tools form

**2. Review all generations before finalization or presentation**
- Example: You generate a massing study concept in ChatGPT, then refine and verify it in Rhino before presenting

**3. Anonymize confidential data**
- Example: Instead of saying "Design a landscape for the Pinehurst Tech Campus," you prompt: "Design a courtyard for a 100,000 sq ft tech office in a temperate climate"

**4. Credit and disclose when AI tools are used in the majority or when mass AI assistance is obtained without partial original authorship**
- Example: On a proposal board, you include: "Visual created using AI image editing tools"

**5. Use secure accounts**
- Example: You log into Runway using the Keeper login instead of your personal email

**6. Consult IT or legal for edge cases**
- Example: You want to test a new platform for 3D-to-video generation. Before uploading, you ask your BIM lead and IT team for approval

### 4.1.3 DON'Ts

**1. Avoid using personal or personal paid accounts for Pfluger work. Only use your Pfluger email tied to a Pfluger account**
- Example: You use your personal paid Chat GPT account to help write a narrative and accidentally share personal conversations or vice versa

**2. Don't upload proprietary designs, models, or internal documents without approval**
- Example: You drop a full Revit model into a free AI object recognition site to "speed up tagging." That model now lives on their servers

**3. Don't rely on AI for legal, contractual, or safety-critical content**
- Example: You ask an AI to draft zoning language for a public submission and submit it without review—it contains errors that put the project at risk

**4. Don't misrepresent AI outputs as fully human-generated**
- Example: You present a fully AI-generated concept render as your own original without mentioning AI use. This misleads stakeholders and opens to authorship liability and copyright

**5. Don't train or fine-tune AI using internal firm data**
- Example: You try to improve an AI model by feeding it real site photos and drawings from confidential projects—these could be leaked or misused

### 4.1.4 Avoid Altogether

**1. Using unvetted or unknown AI tools**
- Example: You find a "free AI render fixer" online and upload a concept, only to realize it shares everything you upload with third parties

**2. Sharing client names, locations, specs, or visuals externally**
- Example: You post an AI-enhanced video of a design still under NDA on your personal social media to show off your work

**3. Bypassing design review**
- Example: You let a text-to-video tool generate a walkthrough, skip team review, and send it to the client—it includes inaccurate semantics
